title: What is known about 1RB0RC_1LC0RE_0LD0LB_1RA1LE_1LB1RF_---0RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RC_1LC0RE_0LD0LB_1RA1LE_1LB1RF_---0RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

It is a binary counter in disguise. The cells just left of the head hold digits written as pairs 00 and 11, and the head's excursions follow the ruler sequence of a counter. Each overflow adds two cells to a solid block at the left end, so the time between overflows doubles, and moves a small marker one step to the right. When the marker reaches the end of its track, the counter is rebuilt and a new, longer epoch starts.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 10,000 steps by the kernel alone and in the first 107 with native_decide; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 2·1010 steps.
Where a halt would come from. The machine halts only in state F reading 0, and F is entered only from E reading 1 and moving right. In 108 steps F is entered 9.5 million times and always reads a 1.

Why it has not halted, and what a proof needs. The run is very regular: a counter whose overflows come exactly twice as far apart each time. A proof would describe one counter cycle and one epoch change symbolically (shift rules for the counter, an induction over the digits) and show that every epoch hands the next one a tape of the same shape. That has not been done; the epoch change is not yet understood in full.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 183 cells have been visited and 108 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Overflows double
claims.text: Each time the head is at the left end in state D the tape starts D>0 0 1^(2n+1) 0, and n goes up by one from one such time to the next within an epoch. The gaps between them double: for example 58,949,630, then 117,899,246, then 235,798,526 steps.

claims.title: Epochs, as digit strings
claims.text: At every overflow (D at the left end) the tape after D>0 0 is a string of odd blocks 1^(2d+1) separated by single 0s; read it as digits d. The first digit goes up by one per overflow and falls back to 0 at an epoch restart, which happens at steps 5, 54, 233, 846, 3,829, 17,354, 22,706,655 and 81,579,964 in the first 108 steps (first digit before the restart 0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 20, 19). Within the epoch that starts at 17,354 the rest of the string is a field of 0 digits with a marker digit that alternates 2, 1, 2, 1, … and moves right 3 places per 2 overflows; the epoch ends when the marker reaches the digits 1 0 0 1 at the right end (… 2 3). The restart rewrites the whole string, e.g. at step 22,706,655 to 0 1 0 2 0 2 0 6 0 3 0…0 1 0 0 1, and at 81,579,964 to 0 1 12 1 0…: the left part of the string is itself a slowly changing higher-level counter, so the epoch-to-epoch map does not keep one fixed shape with growing parameters.

claims.title: A binary counter
claims.text: Between overflows, the cells left of the head read as pairs 00 and 11, and the leftward excursions of the head have the lengths of a ruler sequence (2, 4, 2, 6, 2, 4, 2, 8, … in steps of 2 cells), the pattern of carries in a binary counter.

claims.title: F always reads 1
claims.text: F, the state with the halting transition, is entered only from E reading 1 (1RF); in the first 108 steps it is entered 9,523,781 times and reads a 1 every time.

claims.title: A twin machine
claims.text: 1RB1LE_1RC0RD_1LD0RE_0LA0LC_1LC1RF_---0RA, another holdout, is this machine with its states renamed (A→D, B→A, C→B, D→C) and so started in a different state. Its run settles into the same pattern: at its left-end events (state A at the left end, this machine's D) its tape equals this machine's 77 steps later, except that it ends in 1 0 1 0 1 where this one ends in 1 0 1 0 1^3 (checked at step 553,148,029 against 553,148,106).

claims.title: A run-length frame map, every case proved
claims.text: At every head turn write the tape as two lists of runs (blocks of equal cells), left and right of the head: a frame with list parameters. A table of 69 cases, each a pattern on the first few runs of both sides (lengths exact or at least 4, the rest of each side any list), sends each frame to the frame of the next head turn; every case is proved for all values of its parameters and all lists by one symbolic run (RLCase.sound), so the frame map next = rlNext cases is sound (rlNext_sound). Between two head turns this machine crosses only a few run boundaries, which is why a finite table covers a tape whose number of runs grows without bound.
claims.where: cases, lean/Cases.lean; the runs in lean/Pieces.lean; generated by py/frames.py lean with tools/py/bbtools/listframe.py; library tools/lean/TM/ListFrame.lean

claims.title: The frame map from blank tape
claims.text: The run from blank tape reaches the first frame (init_f0, kernel), and the frame map is defined for its first 1,000,000 frames (native_decide). If it is defined forever along this orbit, the machine never halts (no_halt_of_total).

claims.title: The case table covers the run
claims.text: Every frame at a head turn in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps (3,333,288 head turns) is matched by a case, and the case's next frame is the machine's (no mismatch, no unmatched frame); all 69 cases appear in the first 10<sup>5</sup> steps; none was added up to 10<sup>7</sup>.

claims.title: No finite frame map with scalar parameters
claims.text: The frame-map method (stop at head turns, match the tape against finitely many templates with block-length parameters, fit affine cases) needs the tapes at head turns to fall into a bounded number of shapes. Here they do not: tokenizing the tape at every 7th head turn into maximal powers of words of length at most 4, the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps give 454,843 distinct shapes (exponents of 3 and more merged), 409,534 of them new in the last decade, and up to 36 tokens per tape; the number grows tenfold per decade of steps. For comparison the same count saturates at 32 shapes of at most 5 tokens for 1RB1LC_1LC1RD_1LA0LB_0RB1RE_1RF0RA_---0RC and at 89 for 1RB1RF_1LC1LF_0RE1LD_0LB1LD_---1RC_1RA0RD, where frame maps were proved. The cause is the counter itself: its digits form an arbitrary word, and the word of higher digits on the right grows too, so a frame needs a list parameter; the run-length frames above are such frames.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/power
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.152). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The run looks like a counter that never stops, but the step from one epoch to the next has not been described exactly, let alone proved.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB1LE_1RC0RD_1LD0RE_0LA0LC_1LC1RF_---0RA up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine runs a binary counter: every overflow takes twice as long as the last. This page runs the real machine in your browser, describes the counter, and lists what is known.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Each overflow at the left end comes twice as many steps after the last.
The counter restarts six times in the first 17,354 steps, then at 2.27·10<sup>7</sup> and 8.16·10<sup>7</sup>; the next epoch is still running at 1.5·10<sup>10</sup>.

sections.heading: A counter in pairs of cells
html: Stop the simulator at a random moment after a few million steps and look at the cells left of the head. They read as pairs, 00 and 11: the digits of a binary number. The head runs left over the digits, flipping 11s to 00s until it finds a 00 to turn into 11, then comes back. That is adding one in binary, and the lengths of the head's leftward trips, 2, 4, 2, 6, 2, 4, 2, 8, … cells, are the carry pattern of a counter.

When every digit is 11 the carry runs to the left end and the counter overflows: the solid block at the left end grows by two cells, D>0 0 1^(2n+1) becomes D>0 0 1^(2n+3), and the next overflow takes twice as long. Measured: 58,949,630 steps between two overflows, then 117,899,246, then 235,798,526.

sections.heading: A marker and epochs
html: Each overflow also moves a small block, 1^3, 1^5 or 1^7, one 10 further right through a long run 1 0 1 0 1 0 … on the right part of the tape. When it reaches the end of that run the tape is rewritten and the left block falls back to a single 1: a new epoch starts. After six short early epochs (restarts at steps 5, 54, 233, 846, 3,829 and 17,354), one epoch ends at step 22,706,655 (left block 1^41), the next at step 81,579,964 (1^39); the one after that has reached 1^45 by step 1.5·1010, and at the present rate its 20 or so remaining overflows will take far more steps than anyone can simulate.
So the tape grows only logarithmically in time, which is why the run looks stuck at a small width: about 180 cells after 109 steps.

The holdout 1RB1LE_1RC0RD_1LD0RE_0LA0LC_1LC1RF_---0RA has the same table with the states renamed, and a different start state; its run follows this one 77 steps ahead, with a slightly different right end of the tape.

sections.heading: What a halt would need
html: The only halting transition is F reading a 0. F is entered only from E reading a 1 and stepping right, so the machine halts when E reads a 1 whose right neighbour is 0. In the first 108 steps F is entered 9,523,781 times, always onto a 1: the counter's digits and the marker track never offer E that pattern. Showing that they never will is the open part; it needs an exact description of how one epoch hands over to the next.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.152). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 183 cells (158 left of the start, 22 right), with a density of 1s of 0.59.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: binary counter with a walking marker, in epochs
summary: A binary counter (digits 00/11) that doubles its time with each new left cell, while a marker walks right one step per overflow; when the marker runs out the run restarts on a larger scale.
